Summary: The paper proposes CertGate, a selective-prediction gate for multi-site clinical risk models that treats the site (hospital) rather than the record as the unit of statistical independence. Each calibration site is reduced to a bounded influence-weighted atom Z_c (influence cap M=100), and a Waudby-Smith–Ramdas betting martingale tests whether the site-population influence-weighted answered-set risk R_M exceeds a budget α; a fixed-sequence (learn-then-test) walk over a 23-point threshold grid, ordered on an auxiliary split, selects the operating threshold without δ-splitting. Two assumption modes are offered: an exchangeable baseline and a BBSE label-shift mode whose four estimated parameters (c0, c1, π_source, q_target) carry a Bonferroni-split uncertainty box tested at both odds-ratio endpoints. A linear (L2 logistic) head gives every answer and abstention exact additive attributions and a margin-to-answer decomposition. Validation is on a 208-site synthetic cohort (E1 validity, E2 label shift, E3 verified-falsifiable concept-shift control, E4 site-count frontier, E5 explanations, E6 per-site coverage and three-way answered-set composition, E7 record-as-unit comparator, plus an M-sensitivity sweep) and on eICU-CRD v2.0 (164,322 stays, 207 hospitals) under a protocol frozen before the extract was read, with predictions, failure criteria and leak screens; α=0.10 certifies on all 20 by-site re-splits at 0.890 coverage while α=0.05 never certifies, and the answered set's mortality (0.046) is disclosed against the pool's (0.090).
Strengths: Addresses a real and under-served problem: record-level selective-risk certificates are silently overconfident under site-clustered clinical deployment; the site-as-unit framing is the right one and is aligned with TRIPOD-Cluster / internal-external validation practice.

The estimand construction is clean and careful: the linearized per-site atom Z_c is tied term-by-term to R_M so that E[Z] <= alpha iff R_M <= alpha, non-answering sites enter as neutral atoms, and the paper exhibits why naive truncation of realized contributions is anti-conservative (kept as a regression test).

Unusually honest guarantee text and validation design: the dispersion, parameter-not-count, shared-event, operative-rung and concept-shift clauses travel with the certificate; the negative control (E3) is verified capable of failing before it is run; the record-as-unit comparator (E7) is run on the same draws; the influence cap is swept (Sec. 4.9); the composition instrument exposes when a budget is met by answering easy negatives.

The real-data study is done with pre-frozen protocol, pre-declared predictions and failure criteria, leak screens (one of which fired in the unexpected direction and is reported as such), falsified predictions reported as falsified, and an external clinical comparator (APACHE-IVa) on the answered set.
Reproducibility is strong: released code, one protocol seed, constants pinned by a unit test, byte-identical certificates; aggregate-only artifacts under the PhysioNet DUA.
Weaknesses: Methodological novelty is incremental. Reducing each site to a bounded atom and applying the WSR betting test plus a fixed-sequence LTT walk is a direct application of existing tools; the BBSE-with-uncertainty-box pattern is borrowed from Si et al.; the 'exact attributions' are just w_j(x_j - mu_j) for a logistic head. The paper concedes as much, but for a prestigious ML venue the contribution is closer to an engineering/validation study than a new method.

No comparison to alternative cluster-level certifiers. The only comparator (E7) is the same betting machinery at record granularity. There is no empirical comparison to simpler cluster-level bounds (Hoeffding or empirical-Bernstein over the same Z_c, cluster-bootstrap intervals) nor to hierarchical-conformal / Dunn-Wasserman-Ramdas / Lee-Barber-Willett style procedures or Yu & Liu adapted to site atoms, so the reader cannot tell what the betting martingale buys in coverage or site-count frontier.

The practically achievable certificate has weak content. At ~9% prevalence the operative rung alpha=0.10 exceeds the eICU pool prevalence (0.0889); on the published split the answered 0-1 error is 0.0419 against an answered-set mortality of 0.0458, and the post-hoc panel's skill margin over the constant always-negative rule is 0.0039 - i.e., on the set it answers, the certified head barely improves on predicting 'survives'. The gate reaches its budget partly by abstaining where deaths concentrate. The rung that would be clinically meaningful (alpha=0.05) is unreachable at every tested scale and every M. The paper discloses all this, but it substantially limits the significance of the headline '20/20 certified' result.

The label-shift mode is not shown to be usable: it declines 200/200 draws at the anchor shift, certifies only 9% of draws at the null point (versus 100% for the baseline), and returns failsafe on eICU. Its bootstrap box is asymptotic with measured joint miscoverage 0.038 against a nominal <=0.019, so the 'finite-sample 1-delta' claim in the abstract does not hold for that mode as implemented. Contribution 2 is therefore evidenced mainly by honest refusal, not by a working correction.

The motivating record-vs-site evidence is weaker than the framing suggests. In E7 at the default heterogeneity s_u=0.5 the record-unit certifier grants alpha=0.05 and violates its aggregate budget in only 3.5% of draws (< delta); the ~2*delta failure occurs at s_u=2.0. Yet the eICU per-site dispersion diagnostic (0.027) came in below even the synthetic default (0.055). The paper should reconcile 'record-level certificates are overconfident' with its own evidence that at realistic heterogeneity the record-level certifier stayed within budget while granting a stricter rung.

Validity in E1 is not a stringent test of the certificate: mean fresh-pool R_M is 0.057 against alpha=0.10, so certificates hold with large slack. There is no level/power analysis at the boundary (true risk just above alpha) showing the false-certification rate approaches but does not exceed delta; E7 at s_u=2.0 is the only place the machinery is stressed. The E4 'frontier' (150 sites for alpha=0.10) is a property of this head's risk-coverage curve on an easy generator (sep=2.2), not of the method, and should be framed that way.

Single real cohort, 20 re-splits of one hospital population, no external cohort (e.g., MIMIC or another multi-site registry); the authors acknowledge this cannot estimate a violation rate. Sensitivity/specificity/PPV/NPV of the head on the eICU answered set at the y-hat threshold are not reported in the main text although they are for the synthetic arm.

Clarity/presentation: 25 dense pages with idiosyncratic vocabulary ('rungs', 'atoms', 'walk', 'failsafe', 'poison', 'honest'), very long captions (Table 2), no formal theorem statement in the main text (the validity argument is deferred to SI A.1), and Figure 1 rendered as a text schematic. The repeated 'the system working rather than failing' rhetoric reads defensively.
Questions: What does the betting martingale buy over simpler cluster-level bounds (Hoeffding / empirical-Bernstein / cluster bootstrap) on the same site atoms Z_c, and over hierarchical-conformal or Yu-Liu style procedures adapted to sites? Please report certify rate, coverage and the site-count frontier for at least one such baseline.

Please reconcile E7 with the motivating claim: at s_u=0.5 the record-unit certifier grants alpha=0.05 with 3.5% aggregate violation (< delta), and eICU dispersion (0.027) is below the synthetic default. Can the record-as-unit comparator be run on the eICU re-splits, and what happens?

Report sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV of the head on the eICU answered set at the p-hat >= 1/2 threshold, per re-split, and the answered-set mortality per re-split beside the answered error, so the reader can judge how much the certified head improves on the always-negative rule where it answers.

Assumption 1 requires E[Z_t | F_{t-1}] = E[Z]. The eICU study draws 74 calibration hospitals without replacement from a fixed population of 207 and re-splits it 20 times; does the with-replacement WSR test remain valid here, or should the without-replacement variant be used? Please state the effect on the level.

BBSE mode: how is Z_c(rho) kept in [0,1] for rho up to ~2 (the eICU box reaches 1.986)? Please state the affine-in-rho argument in the main text, and quantify the effective level of the BBSE certificate given the measured 0.038 joint miscoverage of the box.

At what target-pool size and site count would the BBSE mode certify a non-trivial fraction of draws under a moderate shift (e.g., 0.095 -> 0.13)? Certifying 9% at the null point suggests the mode is not usable at practical scale.
How does the E4 frontier move with a weaker head (e.g., AUC 0.75) or a stronger black-box head on eICU (e.g., gradient boosting) - does coverage or the reachable rung change materially?
Why a 2,000-record subsample of S_cal for the record-unit comparator, and is it sampled uniformly over records (over-representing large sites)?
Limitations: The authors state their limitations thoroughly (site-population rather than per-site guarantee; concept shift out of scope; no covariate-shift mode; unmodeled temporal common shocks; symmetric loss and inherited p-hat=1/2 operating point; single real cohort; BBSE intervals asymptotic; cross-hospital patients unfiltered).

Not sufficiently foregrounded: at ~9% prevalence the certified budget alpha=0.10 is weak relative to a constant predictor and the head barely improves on always-negative on the set it answers; a deployer could read the certificate as far more informative than it is. The stricter, meaningful rung is unreachable at realistic site counts, which bounds the practical value.
The label-shift mode's practical usefulness is undemonstrated (declines everywhere it matters), and its finite-sample claim does not hold as implemented.

Potential negative societal impact: a population-average certificate can coexist with individual hospitals running at ~0.29 answered error (as observed), and abstention concentrates on the sickest patients; the equity analysis covers site size only, not hospital type or patient subgroups on real data.
